Change this, see that.

849 cases of a change and what byakugan says about it, from a case-only rename to a new export * line or a Tailwind class in a file nobody imports. Every row links to the test that asserts it.

849 cases
Exports, barrels and code244 cases npm packages, lockfiles and resolution179 cases CSS, Sass and Tailwind143 cases Files, renames, deletions and links121 cases Frameworks and workspaces107 cases Git mode, manifests and --each55 cases
Reading a row

affected means byakugan affected --base main reports a change, or the fingerprint moves. unaffected means neither happens. Some rows name the reason key the test checks, such as src/lib.ts#price for one declaration or npm:lodash for a package. Rows run in the default behavior mode unless they say strict.

Most cases come in pairs: a change that counts next to one that does not. Renaming Hello.ts to hello.ts is affected when main.ts imports ./Hello. Renaming Unused.ts to unused.ts is not.

244 cases

Exports, barrels and code

This page covers edits inside project source files. It shows which exports, imports, top-level statements and comments count, and which do not.

Every row runs in the default behavior mode. Most rows commit a small app with src/main.ts as the entry, edit the working tree and run git mode against main. A row that names a reason shows the key the test asserts.

An unused export next to a used one

byakugan splits a file into declarations and counts only the ones the app reaches. A private helper counts when a used export calls it, and the reason names the helper, not the file.

// src/utils.ts
const pad = (n: number) => String(n).padStart(2, '0');
export function formatDate(date: Date) { return `${date.getFullYear()}-${pad(date.getMonth() + 1)}`; }
export function formatMoney(value: number) { return `$${value.toFixed(2)}`; }
export const cn = (...names: string[]) => names.join(' ');

// src/main.tsx imports formatDate from './utils', and Button uses cn

Deleting or renaming an export

Deleting an export, or dropping its export keyword, counts only when some module imports that name.

// src/main.ts
import { price } from './lib';
console.log(price(2));

// src/lib.ts
export const price = (n: number) => n * 2;
export const other = 1;

Exports of an entry

Every export of an entry counts, because a framework may read it. A Next.js route handler exports GET, POST and revalidate, and no project file imports them.

// src/main.ts, the entry
export const revalidate = 60;
export function GET() { return 'ok'; }
export function POST() { return 'posted'; }
const spare = 1;

Barrels

A barrel line counts when a name the app imports passes through it. A named re-export of a component nobody imports stays out of the graph, and so does an export * line that forwards only unused names.

Every module behind an export * still runs when the barrel runs. Its top-level statements count even when the app uses none of its exports. See limits, "Modules a barrel loads still run".

// src/components/index.ts
export * from './Button';
export * from './Modal';
export { Card } from './Card';

// src/components/Button.tsx, imported by the app through the barrel
Button.displayName = 'Button';

// src/components/Modal.tsx, imported by nobody
export function Modal() { return <div>{formatMoney(10)}</div>; }
Modal.displayName = 'Modal';

export * in an entry

An entry passes on every name its export * lines forward, so they all count. export * never forwards a default export, so a default export behind it does not count, even in an entry.

// src/main.ts, the entry
export * from './config';
export const GET = () => 'ok';

// src/config.ts
export const revalidate = 60;
export const dynamic = 'force-static';

export type * from './analytics';    // analytics.ts logs at the top level
export { track } from './track';

export * cycles and long chains

byakugan follows export * lines through cycles and through thousands of modules, and still counts only the names the app takes.

// src/a.ts
export const a = 1;
export * from './b';

// src/b.ts
export const b = 2;
export * from './a';

// src/index.ts imports b through d.ts (export * from './a')
// and a through c.ts (export * from './b')

Namespace imports

byakugan reads ns.price as a use of price alone. A namespace that comes through export * as ns in a barrel counts whole, so every export behind it counts.

// src/main.ts
import * as ns from './lib';
export const r = ns.price(1);

Imports that run modules

Importing a module runs it, whether or not the app uses the binding. Adding or removing an import counts when the target, or a module it imports, has top-level code. byakugan records the ordered effectful imports of a module in its <imports> fragment.

// src/main.ts
import { Used } from './components';
console.log(Used);

// src/components.ts
import { X } from './some-module';   // the import being added or removed
export const Used = 1;
export const Unused = () => X;       // only an unused export reads X

analytics.ts has console.log('tracking') at the top. fancy.ts imports ./fancy.css. pure.ts only declares export const pure = 1.

The runtime provides bun and cloudflare:workers, so the bundle never ran their code. Dropping an unused import of one does not count.

export const unused = () => x;

Removing an import

Git mode checks a removed import against the base side, since that side ran the module. A bare import of a module that runs belongs to the importer's <module> fragment, so removing it counts even when the target is empty.

// src/main.ts
import './polyfill';
import { price } from './lib';
console.log(price(1));

// src/lib.ts
import './register';          // register.ts is `export {};`
const rate = 2;
export const price = (n: number) => n * rate;
export const legacy = () => 'old';

Removed imports whose target also changed

If git mode checked the removed target in the working tree, where it is gone or now pure, it would call these unaffected. The base side ran the side effect, so the removal counts.

// src/components.ts
import { Fancy } from './fancy';     // fancy.ts: console.log('fancy boot')
export const Used = 1;
export const Unused = () => Fancy;

Each change removes the import line from components.ts, plus the change listed.

Import cycles

A module in an import cycle runs the side effects that any module in the cycle reaches.

// src/a.ts
import { b } from './b';
import { c } from './c';   // c.ts may or may not log at the top level
export const a = () => [b, c];

// src/b.ts
import { a } from './a';
export const b = () => a;
ChangeResultTest
main.ts adds import { b } from './b', used only in an unused local, and c.ts logsaffected, reason src/main.ts#<imports>precision.test.ts:908
Same import, c.ts has no side effectunaffectedprecision.test.ts:914

Lower-level checks of graph.effectful back this up. b.ts reaches the side effect of c.ts only through the cycle and still reads as effectful (precision.test.ts:868). Every member of the cycle gets the same answer whichever is asked first (precision.test.ts:879). A cycle with no side effect anywhere is not effectful (precision.test.ts:889, packaging.test.ts:214), and one with console.log in c.ts makes both a.ts and b.ts effectful (packaging.test.ts:206).

Import order across files

ESM runs imports depth first. An import of a module that already ran still counts when it moves that module earlier, ahead of code that reads what it sets.

// src/main.ts
import './a';     // a.ts imports './x', and x.ts reads globalThis.flag
import './y';     // y.ts imports t.ts, and t.ts sets globalThis.flag = 1
ChangeResultTest
x.ts adds import { t } from './t', used only in an unused exportaffectedprecision.test.ts:1065
Same edit, but main.ts imports ./y before ./aunaffectedprecision.test.ts:1071

In the second order y.ts already ran t.ts before x.ts, so nothing moves.

Top-level code that runs on load

Member assignments

An assignment to a property of a local declaration belongs to that declaration. An assignment on a DOM node reached through a local is a side effect of the module.

Initializers

A top-level initializer that calls a function runs when the module loads, whether or not anything uses the result. Calls that byakugan knows only build a value, such as cva() or a call marked /*#__PURE__*/, count only when the result is used. That assumption can miss a call with side effects. See limits.

// src/lib.ts, main.ts imports only `price`
import { cva } from 'class-variance-authority';
import { createStore } from './store';        // createStore writes to globalThis
export const price = (n: number) => n * 2;
export const store = createStore('a');
export const variants = cva('a');

Declaration order

Moving a const, let or class below the top-level code that reads it throws at runtime, so the move counts. Function declarations are hoisted, and a reference inside a function body runs later, so order does not matter for them.

// src/lib.ts, main.ts imports `price`
export const base = 1;
export const price = base * 2;
export const other = 3;

TypeScript import elision and verbatimModuleSyntax

TypeScript drops an import that brings in only types. Under verbatimModuleSyntax it keeps import { type X } as a bare import, so the module still runs. import type { X } is dropped either way.

// src/theme.ts
document.documentElement.dataset.theme = 'dark';
export type Theme = 'dark' | 'light';

// src/main.ts
import { type Theme } from './theme';
export const t: Theme = 'dark';

The change edits 'dark' to 'light' in the top-level statement of theme.ts.

Decorators and class bodies

Decorators run when the class is defined, so a decorator argument counts even when the app imports no class from the file.

// src/dec.ts
export const Controller = (path) => (target) => { target.path = path; };
export const Input = (name) => (target, key) => {};

// src/users.ts
import { Controller } from './dec';
@Controller('/users')
export class UserController {}

Classic JSX factories and pragmas

With the classic runtime, <div /> calls the factory, so the factory counts. With the automatic runtime (react-jsx) an imported h goes unused, and editing it does not count.

// src/jsx.ts
export const h = (t, p) => ({ t, p });
export const f = (t, p) => [t, p];
export const Fragment = 'frag';

// src/main.tsx, the entry
import { h } from './jsx';
export const App = () => <div />;

require.context and import.meta.webpackContext

byakugan reads the directory and the file pattern off the call. Files that match count. A file added to or deleted from that directory counts too.

// src/main.ts
const icons = require.context('./icons', false, /\.svg$/);
export const names = icons.keys();
// files: src/icons/a.svg, src/icons/b.svg, src/other/c.svg

Deep code and long chains

Deep nesting and long import chains keep the per-declaration split. A file too deep to split falls back to one hash for the whole file, with a warning, so any edit in it counts.

// src/payload.ts
export const x = [[[[ /* 3,000 levels */ ]]]];   // nothing imports x
export const run = () => console.log('v1');      // src/index.ts uses run

Comments and formatting that count

Whitespace counts where JavaScript reads it. A line break after return triggers automatic semicolon insertion and changes the result. Comments that a tool reads count: #__PURE__, webpack magic comments, @vite-ignore, @ts-expect-error, @ts-nocheck, @vitest-environment, /*! legal */ and coverage hints. Parentheses count when they change precedence or end an optional chain. Files in node_modules keep their raw text, comments included.

npm packages, lockfiles and resolution

This page covers code that lives outside the project's own files, and how byakugan resolves an import to a file. It includes npm packages, lockfiles, patches, workspace packages, tsconfig paths and imports that do not resolve.

A named lodash import

lodash is CommonJS, so byakugan hashes each of its files whole. It rewrites import { partition } from 'lodash' to lodash/partition, as Next.js does by default with modularizeImports. Only partition.js and the helpers it requires join the graph, and the 540 KB lodash.js that main names stays out.

// package.json
{ "dependencies": { "lodash": "4.17.21", "es-utils": "1.0.0", "react": "19.0.0" } }
// src/main.tsx
import { partition } from 'lodash';
import { pick } from 'es-utils';

A default import, import _ from 'lodash', uses the whole file. See limits.

An ESM package with sideEffects: false

In an ES module package byakugan goes down to single declarations. The package's sideEffects: false lets it skip the files of a barrel that the app does not take a name from.

// node_modules/es-utils/package.json
{ "type": "module", "sideEffects": false, "exports": { ".": { "import": "./index.js" } } }
// node_modules/es-utils/index.js
export { pick } from './pick.js';
export { omit } from './omit.js';
export * from './keys.js';
// node_modules/es-utils/internal.js
export const hasKey = ...;    // pick and omit use it
export const isObject = ...;  // nothing uses it

Files inside npm packages

The fingerprint and manifest mode look at the files in node_modules that the app reaches. Git mode does not see node_modules, so it reads package changes from the lockfile, one package at a time. The next section covers that.

These rows save a manifest, edit node_modules, and compare against the manifest. The setup is the lodash app above or the monorepo fixture, whose app also imports partition.

The lockfile bump in the second row is affected in git mode, as the next section shows. Manifest mode ignores it because the files partition reaches did not change. A framework package such as next is the exception, since its version counts.

Lockfiles

In git mode byakugan diffs the lockfile and lists the packages whose entry changed. A changed package counts when the app uses it. A new version, integrity, patch hash or git commit each counts as a change, even at the same version. Git mode works per package, so any change to lodash's entry counts once the app uses lodash at all. See limits.

Dependency ranges in package.json

package.json and tsconfig of a workspace package

The package.json and tsconfig.json of a workspace package the app reaches are inputs. Those of a package the app never imports are not. A workspace package's own tsconfig paths apply to its own files.

import { cx } from '~/cx';   // resolves to packages/ui/src/v1/cx.ts

The last row under-counts on purpose. byakugan never reads a base config outside the repository, so its compiler options do not apply. See limits.

Imports byakugan cannot resolve

An import byakugan cannot resolve could hide anything, so it fails closed. The app counts as affected on every run, even for a README edit, and even against a manifest of the same graph. This mostly happens with an alias that only a bundler config defines. Moving the alias into tsconfig or jsconfig paths fixes it. See limits.

// next.config.ts: byakugan does not read it
export default { turbopack: { resolveAlias: { '~lib': './lib' } } };
// app/page.tsx
import { v } from '~lib/v';

Which names fail closed and which warn

byakugan trusts a package that some package.json declares, installed or not, because the lockfile covers it. An undeclared bare name that does not resolve may be a bundler alias, so it fails closed. An import type that does not resolve only warns, since types never run.

virtual in byakugan.json

virtual lists specifiers that a bundler plugin provides. byakugan stops failing closed for the ones it matches. In these globs * stops at /, so ~icons/** is needed for a nested path.

// src/main.ts, a Vite app
import IconHome from '~icons/mdi/home';
import routes from '~react-pages';
// byakugan.json
{ "virtual": ["~icons/**", "~react-pages"] }

Next.js server-only and tsconfig shims

Next.js ships its own copy of server-only, so an import of it that does not resolve does not fail closed. A local shim that a tsconfig alias names is a project file and counts.

// app/page.tsx
import 'server-only';
// tsconfig.json
{ "compilerOptions": { "paths": { "server-only": ["./src/shims/server-only.ts"] } } }
// src/shims/server-only.ts
console.log('shim');

Type-only packages

Several installed copies

Each importer resolves its own copy. A copy that no used code imports does not count.

// src/index.ts
import type { A } from 'zod';           // node_modules/zod 3.0.1
import type { B } from '../lib/x';      // lib/x.ts imports a type from lib/node_modules/zod 4.1.0

Package sideEffects

byakugan believes a package's sideEffects field. A module that the field leaves out drops from the graph when the app uses none of its names, even when it has top-level code.

// src/lib/package.json
{ "sideEffects": ["effect.ts"] }
// src/index.ts
import { e } from './lib/effect';  // e is never used
import { p } from './lib/pure';    // p is never used
export const x = 1;
// src/lib/effect.ts and src/lib/pure.ts both start with console.log(...)
ChangeResultTest
(setup)src/lib/effect.ts#<module> in the graphsecurity.test.ts:241
(setup)src/lib/pure.ts#<module> not in the graphsecurity.test.ts:245

An edit to the console.log in pure.ts would therefore not count.

Fingerprints across machines

CSS, Sass and Tailwind

This page covers stylesheets. It shows which CSS, Sass, Less and Tailwind edits make an app affected, and which ones byakugan ignores.

Most projects below start from this file set unless a snippet says otherwise:

package.json      { "name": "styled" }
byakugan.json     { "entry": ["src/main.ts"] }
.gitignore        node_modules/

"Affected" means byakugan affected --base main reports a change, or the fingerprint changes. A key such as src/app.css#<tailwind> is the reason git mode reports.

CSS imported from code

A stylesheet counts once code the app runs imports it. A stylesheet nobody imports does not count. A module reached only through import type never runs, so the CSS it imports does not ship.

// src/main.ts
import './a.css';
import './b.css';
import 'anim';                          // package exports only { ".": { "style": "./dist/anim.css" } }
import type { Props } from './typed';   // typed.ts does `import './typed.css'`
export const run = (p: Props) => p;
// src/c.css exists, nothing imports it
ChangeResultTest
Edit src/c.cssunaffectedaffected.test.ts:256
Then add import './c.css' to main.tsaffectedaffected.test.ts:256

Edit src/a.cssaffectedaffected.test.ts:264
No edit. import 'anim' names a package whose only export is a style conditionthe graph reaches npm:anim/dist/anim.css, nothing unresolvedaffected.test.ts:272

Order of CSS imports

CSS order decides which rule wins, so moving one CSS import past another counts. Moving it past a module that puts no CSS on the page does not.

// src/main.ts
import './app.css';
import { Header } from './header';      // header.ts imports './header.css'
import styles from './x.module.css';
import { pure } from './pure';          // pure.ts only declares a const
document.body.className = Header + styles.h + pure;

What a stylesheet references

byakugan follows every file a stylesheet names. That covers composes and @value in CSS Modules, Sass @import and @use, Less @import, url() and image-set(). A file named only in a comment does not count.

// src/main.ts
import styles from './button.module.css';
import './main.scss';
import './theme.less';
import './hero.css';
document.body.className = styles.btn;
/* src/button.module.css */
@value primary from './colors.css';
.btn {
  composes: base from './base.module.css';
  color: primary;
}
// src/main.scss
@import 'variables', 'mixins';
// @use 'old';
/* @import 'older'; */
.a { background: url(https://cdn.example.com/a.png); } @use 'tokens';
body { color: $c; }
// src/theme.less
@import (reference) "tokens.less";
.a { color: @brand; }
/* src/hero.css */
.hero { background-image: image-set("./hero.png" 1x, "./hero@2x.png" 2x); }
/* .old { background: url(./old.png); } */

Each row appends a newline to one file and runs git mode.

byakugan resolves stylesheet paths the way the build does. It reads tsconfig paths, sassOptions.includePaths in next.config.js and css.preprocessorOptions.scss.loadPaths in vite.config.ts. Only the file the path resolves to counts, not its siblings.

url() behind an alias, and @value paths

A url() resolves through tsconfig paths like an import. @value with a quoted path names a file. A quoted value that is not a path, such as a font name, stays a string.

// src/main.ts, with tsconfig paths "@/*" -> "./src/*"
import './app.css';
import styles from './button.module.css';
/* src/app.css */
.hero { background: url("@/assets/hero.png"); }
/* src/button.module.css */
@value colors: "./colors.css";
@value font: "Inter";
@value primary from colors;
.btn { color: primary; font-family: font; }

Tailwind v4: class names in files nobody imports

Tailwind scans files the app never imports. byakugan runs the project's Tailwind and hashes the CSS it generates as <root>.css#<tailwind>. A file nobody imports makes the app affected only when it adds a class that changes that CSS.

/* src/app.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
// src/main.ts
import './app.css';
import { button } from './button';   // export const button = 'flex p-4 text-sm';
document.body.className = button;
// src/unused.ts, never imported, but Tailwind scans it
export const banner = () => ['rounded', 'quiet words'];
ChangeResultTest
No editsrc/app.css#<tailwind> is live, src/unused.ts#banner is not, no warningstailwind.test.ts:50

This counts classes, not rendered markup. A class in a component nobody renders yet still changes the CSS. limits.md lists this.

Tailwind v4: @source

@source sets which files Tailwind scans, so it also sets which files can count.

When Tailwind cannot run

If Tailwind fails, byakugan hashes every file Tailwind might scan whole and warns "could not run Tailwind". Plain text edits then count. That costs rebuilds, but no class change slips through. limits.md describes this fallback.

apps/web                                  Next.js app, imports '@workspace/ui/globals.css'
packages/ui/src/styles/globals.css        @import "tailwindcss"; @plugin "./broken.mjs"; @source "../**/*.{ts,tsx}";
packages/ui/src/styles/broken.mjs         throw new Error('boom');
packages/ui/src/components/dialog.tsx     className='rounded skew-y-12'

Vite query imports

The query decides whether comments count. Vite emits a file imported with ?raw or ?url byte for byte, so byakugan hashes its whole text as <raw> and a comment edit counts. Vite bundles a ?worker file like a normal import, so comments and unused exports in its imports do not count. No graph key keeps the ?query.

// src/main.ts, a Vite app with tsconfig paths "~/*" -> "./src/*"
import sheet from '~/app.css?url';
import inline from './inline.css?inline';
import snippet from './snippet.ts?raw';
import { used } from './used';
import Counter from './counter.ts?worker';
export const links = [sheet, inline, snippet, used, new Counter()];
// src/snippet.ts
// shown on the docs page
export const answer = 42;
// src/used.ts
// a helper
export const used = 1;
// src/counter.ts
import { step } from './step';
let count = 0;
self.onmessage = () => postMessage((count += step));
// src/step.ts
export const step = 1;
export const unused = 2;

Files, renames, deletions and links

This page covers files the app reads by path instead of a plain import, and changes to the file tree itself: renames, deletions, ignored files, symlinks and submodules. "Git mode" means byakugan affected --base main. Rows without it compare fingerprints.

Case-only renames

A rename that changes only the case of a file name counts when an import spells the old name. On macOS the import of ./Hello still finds hello.ts, so the app builds locally. A Linux CI runner looks for Hello.ts and fails, so byakugan reports it.

// src/main.ts
import { hello } from './Hello';
console.log(hello());
// src/Hello.ts
export const hello = () => 'hi';
// src/Unused.ts
export const unused = 1;

Rename the directory src/lib to src/Lib while main.ts imports ./lib/greetaffectedgit-mode.test.ts:772

These tests need a case-insensitive file system. They run on macOS and skip on Linux, so Linux CI does not run them.

Deleted files the app still refers to

Deleting a file that an import, a url() or a path in code names is affected, even though the file is no longer there to compare. Git mode matches the deleted path against what the base graph resolved. Deleting a file nothing names is unaffected.

Computed import() patterns

A template import() with a relative prefix becomes a pattern. byakugan adds every file the pattern matches to the graph and records the pattern, so git mode also catches a deleted match.

const x = String(Math.random());

// src/l/1a2b.js matches the pattern
// src/l/zzz.js does not

Patterns byakugan cannot follow

An import() whose template starts with an alias does not become a pattern. byakugan warns and treats the files it might load as outside the graph.

// tsconfig.json paths: "@/*": ["./src/*"]
// src/index.ts
export const load = (l: string) => import(`@/messages/${l}.json`);
ChangeResultTest
Edit src/messages/de.jsonunaffected, warns cannot follow import(...)packaging.test.ts:364

This is a known gap, listed under "Paths byakugan cannot read off the code" in limits. An unresolved static import fails closed and always counts. This one only warns, so add the files to inputs when you see the warning.

import.meta.glob

byakugan matches the glob against the directory it names and adds each match to the graph. Exclusions with ! drop files. A glob or a link that leads outside the repository reads nothing and warns.

// src/index.ts
export const pages = import.meta.glob(['./pages/*.ts', '!./pages/skip.ts']);

Files read through process.cwd()

byakugan reads join(process.cwd(), 'dir', ...) as a path in code and counts the files under it. A path that leaves the repository reads nothing and warns.

import { join } from 'node:path';
export const post = (slug: string) => readFileSync(join(process.cwd(), 'content', slug));

Frameworks and workspaces

This page shows how byakugan finds entries and hidden inputs in each framework it detects, and how it picks the apps of a workspace. Every row comes from a test. frameworks.md has the short version with results from real projects.

Next.js 'use server' files

Every export of a 'use server' file counts, imported or not. Next.js may register each one as a server action endpoint. A plain module next to it keeps per-export precision.

// app/page.tsx
import { save } from './actions';
import { formatPrice } from './lib';

// app/actions.ts
'use server';
export async function save() { return 'saved'; }
export async function remove() { return 'removed'; }

// app/lib.ts
export const formatPrice = (n: number) => '$' + n;
export const formatTax = (n: number) => n * 0.23;
ChangeResultTest
Change 0.23 to 0.08 in formatTax, an export nobody importsunaffectednext.test.ts:121
Change 'removed' to 'deleted' in remove, an export nobody importsaffectednext.test.ts:121

Next.js 'use client' modules and strict

When a server component imports a 'use client' module, Next.js ships that module to the browser whole. The default behavior mode counts only the exports the app can run. strict mode counts every export, since every one of them ends up in the bundle.

// ui/widget.tsx
'use client';
export const Used = () => <b>used</b>;
export const Unused = () => <i>one</i>;

// app/page.tsx, a server component
import { Used } from '../ui/widget';
export default function Page() { return <Used />; }
ChangeResultTest
Change one to two in Unusedaffected (strict)next.test.ts:155, cli.test.ts:187
The same edit in behavior modeunaffectednext.test.ts:159, cli.test.ts:194
Change the text of Used in behavior modeaffectednext.test.ts:163
Change Unused with strict passed by the caller instead of byakugan.jsonaffected (strict)next.test.ts:170
Change Unused when the page reaches widget through ui/panel.tsx and an export * barrel ui/index.tsaffected (strict)next.test.ts:181
Change Unused when the page is itself 'use client'unaffected (strict)next.test.ts:191
Change Unused with framework: 'none'unaffected (strict)next.test.ts:195

Only an import that crosses from a server module into a client module triggers the rule. Client modules that import each other keep per-export precision.

Next.js files reached without a static import

A Next.js app reads many files that no import statement names. byakugan follows computed import() calls, fs reads under process.cwd(), new URL(..., import.meta.url), localFont({ src }) paths and url() in stylesheets.

// app/[locale]/page.tsx
const messages = (await import(`../../messages/${locale}.json`)).default;

// app/legacy/page.tsx
const strings = await import('./locales/' + lang + '.js');

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
await readFile(join(process.cwd(), 'content', 'posts', `${slug}.md`), 'utf8');

// app/worker/page.tsx
new Worker(new URL('./worker.ts', import.meta.url));

// app/fonts.ts
export const brand = localFont({ src: './fonts/brand.woff2' });

// app/computed/page.tsx
return (await import(name)).default;
/* app/globals.css */
@import "style-only";
body { background: url("./bg.png"), url(/hero.png); }

The project also holds messages/en.json, messages/pl.json, data/other.json, content/posts/first.md, content/drafts/draft.md, app/fonts/spare.woff2, app/global-not-found.tsx and i18n/request.ts.

// src/server.ts

  .use('*', cors())
  .use('/static/*', serveStatic({ root: './public' }))

HonoX and import.meta.glob

HonoX's entries are app/server.ts, app/client.ts, the files under app/routes/ and the client inputs vite.config.ts names. HonoX finds routes with import.meta.glob, and byakugan follows that call in any file, negative patterns included.

// vite.config.ts
export default { plugins: [{ client: { input: ['/app/client.ts', '/app/style.css'] } }] };

// app/server.ts
export default import.meta.glob(['/app/pages/*.ts', '!/app/pages/_draft.ts'], { eager: true });

Hono RPC across two apps

A Hono RPC client imports only the server's type. byakugan follows import type through types alone, so the client gets the route declarations, the handlers and the helpers whose return values shape a response. The server's bootstrap code stays out, and so do packages only that code imports. A package the client reaches only through types counts as npm:<pkg>#<types>.

// apps/api/src/index.ts
import 'dotenv/config';
import { serve } from '@hono/node-server';
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { products } from './products';
const app = new Hono().route('/products', products);
export type AppType = typeof app;
serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3001 });

// apps/api/src/products.ts
import { z } from 'zod';
import { listProducts } from './db';
export const products = new Hono().get('/', c => c.json(listProducts(z.string())));

// apps/api/src/db.ts
export const listProducts = (schema: unknown) => [{ id: '1', schema }];
export const resetDatabase = () => 'reset';

// apps/web/src/main.ts
import { hc } from 'hono/client';
import type { AppType } from '@acme/api';
export const client = hc<AppType>('/');
ChangeResultTest

The listProducts edit changes the inferred AppType, so the client counts it even though it never runs server code. There is no type checker, so a handler body edit counts even when the response type stays the same. See limits.md.

SvelteKit

Routes, hooks and config files are entries. $lib resolves before svelte-kit sync writes .svelte-kit/tsconfig.json, and $app/* is not reported as unresolved. SvelteKit inlines every name imported from $env/static/*, so each one counts by value, whatever its prefix.

<!-- src/routes/+page.svelte -->
<script lang="ts">
  import { page } from '$app/state';
  import { price } from '$lib/money';
  import { PUBLIC_SHOP, SECRET_KEY } from '$env/static/private';
</script>
// src/routes/+page.server.ts
import { price } from '$lib/money';

// src/lib/money.ts
export const price = (n: number) => n * 2;
export const tax = (n: number) => n * 0.2;

Vue, Svelte and Astro components

byakugan hashes a .vue, .svelte or .astro file whole, so any edit to the file counts. The modules its scripts import keep per-export precision. In a Vue file, the assets the template names, child components and @import in <style> count too.

<!-- src/App.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
import { Button } from './ui';
import { price } from './money';
import Child from './Child.vue';
</script>
<template>
  <img src="./logo.png" />
  <Button>{{ price(2) }}</Button>
  <Child />
</template>
<style lang="scss">
@import './theme';
</style>
// src/money.ts
export const price = (n: number) => n * 2;
export const tax = (n: number) => n * 0.2;

// src/ui/index.ts
export { Button } from './Button';
export { Card } from './Card';

The Svelte and Astro versions import Button and price the same way. The first four rows run for all three, in git mode.

Environment variables

By default a variable counts when the bundler inlines it and live code reads it. That means NEXT_PUBLIC_* in Next.js, VITE_* in Vite and any $env/static name in SvelteKit. A server-only secret counts only when env in byakugan.json names it.

// lib/config.ts in a Next.js app. app/page.tsx imports only url.
export const url = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_URL;
export const unused = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_UNUSED;
export const secret = process.env.SECRET;

Git mode compares no values, since the base commit has no environment. A variable read by a computed name or from a config file needs an entry in env. limits.md describes both.

Which workspace packages are apps

--workspace runs byakugan once per app. A package counts as a library when another package lists it in dependencies. A package listed only in devDependencies is an app when it has a start script.

// package.json
{ "workspaces": ["packages/*"] }

// packages/e2e/package.json
{ "devDependencies": { "server": "*", "tools": "*" } }
SetupResultTest
server has a start scriptapps e2e and serverworkspace.test.ts:23
server has no start scriptapp e2e onlyworkspace.test.ts:28
e2e lists only server, in dependencies, and server has startapps e2e and tools, server is a libraryworkspace.test.ts:33

In the third row, tools becomes an app because no package lists it any more. The rule is that no other package depends on it, which can catch a package you think of as a library.

A library may have a framework in its dependencies, for example next for its types.

Framework detection in workspaces

byakugan detects an app's framework from the app's own package.json. When the app has none, it reads the root one. A root package can also complete an app that declares only part of a framework.

One parse cache for all workspace apps

The CLI gives every app's graph one module cache, so byakugan parses a shared file once. The cache keys on parse options, so one app's compiler settings never leak into another's graph.

Git mode, manifests and --each

This page shows how byakugan affected picks the two sides it compares, how a saved manifest stands in for the base side, and which files --each selects. Other pages cover what a given code edit means.

Branches and merge base

affected --base main compares the working tree with the merge base of main and HEAD. Commits on your branch count. Commits that landed on main after you branched do not.

The first two rows use the monorepo fixture in test/fixtures/monorepo, a Next.js app in apps/web that renders Hero. The last two use a small app.

// byakugan.json
{ "entry": ["src/main.ts"] }
// src/main.ts
import { greet } from './greet';
console.log(greet());
// src/greet.ts
export const greet = () => 'hi';
ChangeResultTest
On branch feature, commit an edit to components/Unused.tsxunaffectedaffected.test.ts:88
Then commit an edit to components/Hero.tsx on the same branchaffected, reason apps/web/components/Hero.tsx#Heroaffected.test.ts:88
main edits greet.ts after the branch point, feature edits nothing the app usesunaffected, no warningsgit-mode.test.ts:1092
Same history in a shallow clone, where main and feature share no commitaffected, reason src/greet.ts#greet, warns main and HEAD have no merge basegit-mode.test.ts:1098

Without a merge base, byakugan compares against the tip of main. The edit that main made to greet.ts then shows up as yours. The warning says so. Set fetch-depth: 0 on actions/checkout so the clone has the merge base, as ci.md shows.

Manifest mode

hash --manifest <file> saves a hash per fragment. affected --base-manifest <file> compares the current graph with that file instead of reading the base side from git.

ChangeResultTest
Write a manifest, compare the same tree against itunaffectedsecurity.test.ts:947, git-mode.test.ts:1127
The manifest has a fragment __proto__ that the current graph lacksaffected, reason __proto__: no longer usedsecurity.test.ts:930

A fragment that was in the manifest and is gone from the graph is a reason, no longer used.

A manifest records the byakugan version, its format and the mode that wrote it. If any of them differs from the current run, byakugan cannot compare fragment by fragment, so it reports affected with one reason that says why.

--each in git mode

affected --each 'src/**/*.test.ts' makes every matching file a root and prints the ones a change reaches. byakugan walks back from each reason to the test files. A change to the test runner config or package.json selects every test.

// src/math.ts
export const add = (a, b) => a + b;
export const sub = (a, b) => a - b;
export const unused = () => 0;
// src/pad.ts
import pad from 'left-pad';
export const padded = (s) => pad(s, 4);
// src/ui/index.ts
export { Button } from './Button';
export { Card } from './Card';
// src/add.test.ts imports add
// src/sub.test.ts imports sub and padded
// src/button.test.ts imports Button from './ui'
// src/card.test.ts imports Card from './ui'
// also vitest.config.ts, and package.json and package-lock.json with left-pad 1.0.0

The ?raw row counts a comment. A ?raw import hands the test the file's text, so every byte of it counts. Through a normal import, comments do not.

--each against a manifest

hash --each <glob> --manifest <file> also saves one fingerprint per matched file, over the fragments that file reaches. affected --each <glob> --base-manifest <file> then selects the files whose fingerprint moved. Comparing fingerprints works where the walk cannot. A fragment that left the graph gives the walk nowhere to start.

Same setup as the previous section.

Storybook

--each 'src/**/*.stories.ts' selects stories the same way. .storybook/main.ts and whatever .storybook/preview.ts imports reach every story.

// .storybook/main.ts
export default { stories: ['../src/**/*.stories.ts'] };
// .storybook/preview.ts
import { theme } from '../src/theme';
export const parameters = { theme };
// src/button.stories.ts
import { Button } from './ui';
export default { component: Button };
// src/card.stories.ts
import { Card } from './ui';
export default { component: Card };

byakugan compare

byakugan compare <base build dir> <fresh build dir> lists the files that differ between two build outputs. In a Next.js build it drops what changes on every build, so two builds of the same code match.

BUILD_ID
required-server-files.json            outputFileTracingRoot is the checkout path
static/<build id>/_buildManifest.js
server/app/page.js
server/server-reference-manifest.json  holds encryptionKey
cache/
trace

byakugan treats cache/ and trace as noise only in a Next.js build. In other build output they are ordinary files.

Many changed files

Git mode checks each changed fragment on its own, however many files change. An edit counts only if it hits a fragment the app uses.
